intro: String algorithms turn questions about matching, repetition, and symmetry in text into linear- or near-linear-time computations by precomputing structural information once and reusing it for O(1) or O(log n) queries. The core toolkit here — the prefix function (KMP), the Z-function, polynomial hashing, Manacher's algorithm, and tries (with suffix arrays/automata as the natural next step) — covers the overwhelming majority of "hard" string problems on Codeforces, CSES, and LeetCode. Master the mechanics of each precomputed array first; almost every hard problem is a non-obvious reduction on top of one of these arrays rather than a new algorithm.

subtopics.name: KMP Pattern Matching (Prefix Function)
subtopics.theory:
The prefix function pi[i] of a string s is defined as the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of s[0..i] (proper meaning it cannot be the entire substring s[0..i] itself). It is computed in O(n) with a clever amortized argument: to compute pi[i] from pi[i-1], start a candidate match length j = pi[i-1] (the best border known so far) and repeatedly fall back to j = pi[j-1] while s[i] != s[j], exactly the same 'failure link' idea used to avoid re-scanning already-matched characters. Because j can only increase by 1 per iteration of the outer loop but is reset by fallbacks that are bounded by the total increase, the amortized cost over all i is O(n).

The classic application is substring search: concatenate pattern + separator + text (the separator must be a character that occurs in neither string, e.g. '#') and run the prefix function on the combined string. Every position where pi[i] equals the pattern's length marks an occurrence ending there, because a border of length |pattern| at that point means the preceding |pattern| characters of the combined string exactly equal the pattern. This gives O(n + m) pattern matching without ever backtracking in the text, which is what makes KMP asymptotically better than the naive O(n*m) sliding comparison.

Beyond direct matching, the prefix function encodes deep structural information about a string: repeatedly following pi[n-1] -> pi[pi[n-1]-1] -> ... enumerates every border of the whole string, which is exactly the information needed to find all periods of a string (period k works iff n-k is a border length) or to detect that a string is built from repetitions of a smaller block. The same 'prefix function on a concatenation with a separator' trick generalizes far beyond pattern search — e.g. computing the longest palindromic prefix of s by running it on s + '#' + reverse(s).
subtopics.recognition: Reach for KMP/prefix-function whenever you need exact substring matching in O(n+m), need the borders (prefix=suffix) of a string, need the minimal period of a string, or see a problem that can be phrased as 'longest prefix of A that is also a suffix of B' — the giveaway is usually the phrase 'find all occurrences' or 'shortest string with property X built by adding a prefix/suffix', which often reduces to a border query on a cleverly concatenated string.
subtopics.complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space where n = |text|, m = |pattern|.

examples.title: All Occurrences of a Pattern
examples.problem: You are given a text string T (1 <= |T| <= 2*10^5) and a pattern string P (1 <= |P| <= |T|), both consisting of lowercase Latin letters. Find every starting index (0-indexed) at which P occurs in T (occurrences may overlap). Print the number of occurrences, then the 0-indexed starting positions in increasing order on one line separated by spaces.
examples.approach: Build combined = P + '#' + T using a separator character guaranteed not to appear in either string. Compute the prefix function pi of combined in O(|combined|). For every index i in the T-part of combined (i.e. i > |P|), if pi[i] == |P| then a full copy of P ends at position i of combined; converting back to an index in T gives start = i - 2*|P| (subtract |P| for the pattern part and the separator, then |P| more for the length of the match itself: i - 2*|P|). Collect all such starts.

examples.title: Shortest Palindrome by Prefix Addition
examples.problem: Given a string s (1 <= |s| <= 5*10^4) of lowercase Latin letters, you may add characters in front of s to make the whole string a palindrome. Output the shortest palindrome achievable this way.
examples.approach: If we prepend k characters to make s a palindrome, those k characters must equal the reverse of the last k characters of the resulting palindrome, which forces the prepended block to equal reverse(suffix) in a very specific way; the key reduction is: we want the longest prefix of s that is itself a palindrome, because everything after that prefix must be mirrored in front. Compute combined = s + '#' + reverse(s) and run the prefix function; pi.back() gives the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s (it equals the longest border between s and reverse(s), which is exactly the longest prefix of s that reads the same as a suffix of reverse(s), i.e. a palindrome). The characters of s beyond that prefix, reversed, are exactly what must be prepended: answer = reverse(s[longest:]) + s.

examples.title: Finding All Periods of a String
examples.problem: A string s of length n (1 <= n <= 10^6) has period k (1 <= k <= n) if s[i] == s[i+k] for every valid i (0 <= i <= n-k-1). Note k = n is always a trivially valid period. Given s, output all valid periods of s in increasing order, space-separated.
examples.approach: Compute the prefix function pi of s directly (no concatenation needed here). The chain b = pi[n-1], then b = pi[b-1], and so on until b = 0, enumerates every border length of the full string. A border of length b corresponds exactly to period n-b, because s[0..b) == s[n-b..n) means s repeats with period n-b. Collect n-b for every border in the chain, add the trivial period n itself, sort, and print.

subtopics.name: Z-function
subtopics.theory:
The Z-function of a string s is an array z where z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix between s and the suffix of s starting at index i (by convention z[0] is either left undefined or set to n, the whole string trivially matching itself). It is computed in O(n) using the same 'reuse previously computed matches' idea as KMP, but framed differently: maintain a window [l, r) — the rightmost Z-box found so far, i.e. the interval matching a prefix of s that extends furthest to the right. When computing z[i] for i inside the current window, we can initialize z[i] from the already-known value z[i-l] (mirrored inside the prefix) rather than starting from scratch, then only extend by brute-force comparison past the window boundary r. Every successful character comparison beyond r increases r by 1 and never decreases it, which bounds total comparisons to O(n).

The Z-function and the prefix function carry equivalent information (each can be derived from the other in O(n)), but the Z-function is often more natural for problems phrased in terms of 'longest common prefix with the whole string starting at position i', which is a very common way hard problems disguise this technique — e.g. LeetCode's 'Sum of Scores of Built Strings' literally defines score(i) to be the Z-function by another name.

For pattern matching, the same separator trick as KMP applies: build pattern + '#' + text and scan the Z-array for values >= |pattern|, which mark occurrences. Another powerful use is counting, for every prefix length L, how many times that prefix occurs as a substring anywhere in s: increment a counter at z[i] for every i, add one more for the full string itself (which trivially matches its own prefix at position 0), then take a suffix sum over counter values from n down to 1.
subtopics.recognition: Look for the Z-function whenever a problem talks about 'the longest common prefix between the string and one of its suffixes', needs substring occurrence positions, or needs, for every prefix, how often it recurs inside the string. It is functionally interchangeable with KMP for pure pattern matching, so pick whichever framing makes the reduction to the problem's phrasing cleaner.
subtopics.complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space where n = |text|, m = |pattern|.

examples.title: Pattern Matching via the Z-array
examples.problem: Given a text T and a pattern P (both lowercase Latin letters, 1 <= |P| <= |T| <= 2*10^5), find every 0-indexed starting position where P occurs in T. Print the count followed by the sorted starting positions on one line.
examples.approach: Form combined = P + '#' + T and compute its Z-array. For every position i within the T-part (i > |P|), z[i] >= |P| means the substring of combined starting at i shares at least |P| characters with the whole combined string, i.e. with P itself — an occurrence of P in T starting at index i - |P| - 1.

examples.title: Sum of Scores of Built Strings
examples.problem: For a string s of length n (1 <= n <= 10^5), define score(i) as the length of the longest common prefix between s and the suffix of s starting at index i, for every i from 0 to n-1 (score(0) = n since s trivially matches its whole self). Compute the sum of score(i) over all i. (This is LeetCode Hard #2223.)
examples.approach: score(i) is exactly the definition of the Z-function value z[i] for i >= 1, and score(0) = n matches the conventional z[0] = n. So the answer is simply the sum of the entire Z-array (with z[0] set to n). Compute the Z-array in O(n) and sum it — the entire difficulty of this 'hard' problem is recognizing the reduction, not the implementation.

subtopics.name: String Hashing (Polynomial Rolling Hash)
subtopics.theory:
A polynomial hash maps a string s of length n to H(s) = (s[0]*B^(n-1) + s[1]*B^(n-2) + ... + s[n-1]*B^0) mod M for a base B and modulus M. By precomputing prefix hashes h[0..n] (h[i] = hash of s[0..i)) and powers of B, the hash of any substring s[l..r) can be recovered in O(1) via h[r] - h[l]*B^(r-l) (mod M), because shifting the prefix hash of s[0..l) up by (r-l) digits and subtracting cancels out everything before index l. This turns 'are these two substrings equal' into an O(1) integer comparison after O(n) preprocessing, which is the whole appeal: it trades a small, controllable false-positive probability for speed and simplicity that beats writing a suffix structure.

The critical danger is collisions. A single hash modulo a ~10^9 prime, especially with a fixed, well-known base/modulus pair, can be deliberately defeated by adversarial test data (this is a known 'anti-hash test' phenomenon on Codeforces) and even without adversarial input, the birthday bound means collisions become likely once you compare on the order of sqrt(M) substrings. The standard defenses are: (1) double hashing — compute two independent hashes with different (base, modulus) pairs and compare the pair, which squares the safety margin to roughly 10^18; or (2) hash modulo a large prime close to 2^61 with a randomized base chosen at runtime, using 128-bit intermediate multiplication to avoid overflow, which is safe against static anti-hash tests. Never trust a single small-modulus hash in a contest with adaptive or adversarial data.

Hashing also extends naturally to palindrome checking: precompute both the forward hash of s and the forward hash of reverse(s); a substring s[l..r) is a palindrome iff its forward hash equals the forward hash of the mirrored range in reverse(s). This generalizes to dynamic settings (point updates) by replacing the flat prefix-hash array with a Fenwick tree or segment tree that supports point update and range hash query, at the cost of O(log n) instead of O(1) per query.
subtopics.recognition: Use hashing whenever you need fast substring equality checks, longest common substring/prefix queries combined with binary search, palindrome checks on arbitrary ranges (especially under updates, where suffix structures are hard to maintain), or any place you'd like to avoid building a suffix automaton/array but still need 'is this substring equal to that substring' in better than O(length).
subtopics.complexity: O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per substring-hash query (O(log n) with a Fenwick/segment tree for point updates); O(n log n) total for a binary-search-based application.

examples.title: Longest Common Substring (Double Hash + Binary Search)
examples.problem: Given two strings s and t (1 <= |s|, |t| <= 5*10^4, lowercase Latin letters), find the length of their longest common substring, and print one such substring.
examples.approach: The existence of a common substring of length L is monotonic in L: if some common substring of length L exists, truncating one character from both copies gives a common substring of length L-1, so the predicate 'a common substring of length L exists' is true for a prefix of lengths 0..answer and false above. Binary search on L; for the check, hash every length-L substring of s into a set (using a double hash pair to make accidental collisions negligible) and test every length-L substring of t for membership in O(1) per substring. Each check costs O(n+m), giving O((n+m) log n) overall.

examples.title: Prefix-Suffix Palindrome
examples.problem: Given a string s (1 <= |s| <= 10^6) of lowercase Latin letters, find the length of the longest string that can be formed by concatenating a prefix of s and a suffix of s (the prefix and suffix must not overlap, and either may be empty) such that the concatenation is a palindrome. Print the length and one such palindrome. (Based on Codeforces 1326 D2.)
examples.approach: Greedily peel matching outer characters with two pointers i=0, j=n-1: while s[i] == s[j], advance i and retreat j. This gives the maximal 'shell' — a prefix of length shell=i that exactly equals the reverse of the corresponding suffix — which can always be wrapped, unmodified, around any palindrome found in the remaining middle segment s[i..j]. The problem now reduces to: find the longest palindromic PREFIX of the middle or the longest palindromic SUFFIX of the middle (whichever is longer), and sandwich it between the shell and its mirrored copy. Use double hashing to test 'is s[l..r) a palindrome' in O(1) (by comparing the forward hash of that range against the forward hash of the mirrored range in reverse(s)), and scan candidate lengths from the full middle length down to 0, stopping at the first palindrome found — this is O(|middle|) with O(1) checks, no binary search needed since 'is a palindrome' is not itself monotonic in length.

examples.title: Palindrome Queries with Point Updates
examples.problem: You are given a string s (1 <= |s| <= 2*10^5) of lowercase Latin letters and q queries (1 <= q <= 2*10^5) of two types: '1 pos c' — set the character at 1-indexed position pos to c; '2 a b' — output YES if s[a..b] (1-indexed, inclusive) is currently a palindrome, NO otherwise. Process all queries online. (Based on CSES 'Palindrome Queries'.)
examples.approach: A flat prefix-hash array can't handle point updates efficiently (an update would shift every hash after it). Instead build a segment tree over the string where each node stores two hashes of its range under one large-modulus polynomial hash: the forward hash (read left to right) and the reverse hash (as if the range were read right to left). Forward hashes merge as combine(L,R) = L.hash * B^|R| + R.hash. Reverse hashes merge in the opposite order, because reverse(A+B) = reverse(B) + reverse(A): combine(L,R) = R.rev * B^|L| + L.rev. A point update just rewrites a leaf and recomputes O(log n) ancestors; a range query merges O(log n) segment-tree nodes to get the forward and reverse hash of the queried range in O(log n), and the range is a palindrome iff the two hashes are equal. Using a modulus near 2^61 with 128-bit multiplication (or double hashing) keeps collision probability negligible even under adversarial queries.

subtopics.name: Manacher's Algorithm
subtopics.theory:
Manacher's algorithm computes, for every center in a string, the radius of the longest palindrome centered there — for all n centers simultaneously in O(n), rather than the naive O(n^2) of expanding around every center independently. It is usually implemented with two arrays: d1[i], the number of odd-length palindromes centered exactly at index i (so the longest has length 2*d1[i]-1), and d2[i], the number of even-length palindromes centered between indices i-1 and i (longest length 2*d2[i]). Some implementations transform s by inserting separators (e.g. '#') between every character to unify odd and even cases into a single array; the two-array formulation used here avoids that transformation and its associated off-by-one bookkeeping.

The O(n) bound comes from the same 'reuse a previously discovered window' trick as the Z-function: maintain the rightmost palindrome boundary [l, r] found so far. When computing the radius at a new center i inside that window, mirror the already-known radius of the reflected center (l+r-i) to get a lower bound for free — because palindromic symmetry around the center of [l,r] guarantees palindromes on the mirrored side extend at least that far — and only then attempt to extend character by character past the window's edge. Since r only ever moves rightward and each brute-force extension attempt beyond r advances r by one position, the total extension work across all centers is O(n).

Beyond 'find the longest palindromic substring', the d1/d2 arrays are a general-purpose tool: summing them gives the total count of palindromic substrings in O(n) (each value d1[i] or d2[i] counts exactly that many distinct palindromic substrings centered there, since every radius from 1 up to the maximum is itself a valid, shorter palindrome). A subtler but very common transformation is converting 'longest palindrome centered at each position' into 'longest palindrome ENDING at each position' — since a center's maximal palindrome only directly tells you about the single rightmost endpoint it reaches, but every smaller radius from the same center is also a valid palindrome ending at an earlier position, so a two-pointer sweep is needed to correctly propagate the best value forward to every ending index.
subtopics.recognition: Manacher's is the go-to whenever a problem needs palindrome information (existence, count, or longest) for many or all centers/positions in O(n) rather than per-query O(n) or O(n^2) total — the giveaway phrase is usually 'longest palindromic substring', 'count palindromic substrings', or 'longest palindrome ending/starting at position i, for every i'.

examples.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
examples.problem: Given a string s (1 <= |s| <= 10^6) of lowercase Latin letters, find its longest palindromic substring. If multiple substrings of the maximum length exist, output the leftmost one.
examples.approach: Run Manacher's algorithm to get d1 (odd palindromes) and d2 (even palindromes). For each center i, the odd-length candidate has length 2*d1[i]-1 starting at i-d1[i]+1, and the even-length candidate has length 2*d2[i] starting at i-d2[i]. Track the best (length, start) pair using a strict '>' comparison so the first (leftmost) occurrence of the maximum length is kept.

examples.title: Counting All Palindromic Substrings
examples.problem: Given a string s (1 <= |s| <= 10^6), count the total number of palindromic substrings (counting multiplicity — two occurrences of the same palindromic string at different positions count separately).
examples.approach: Every palindrome centered at i with maximum radius d1[i] (odd case) contributes exactly d1[i] distinct palindromic substrings centered there — one for every radius from 1 up to d1[i], since a shorter palindrome sharing the same center is automatically still a palindrome. The same logic gives d2[i] even-length palindromes for each even center. So the total count is simply the sum of the entire d1 array plus the sum of the entire d2 array, computed via one Manacher pass in O(n).

examples.title: Longest Palindrome Ending at Each Position
examples.problem: Given a string s of length n (1 <= n <= 5*10^5), for every index e from 0 to n-1 output the length of the longest palindromic substring of s that ends exactly at index e. (Based on CSES 'All Palindromes'.)
examples.approach: Run Manacher to get d1 and d2. A center c with odd radius d1[c] can produce a palindrome ending at any e with c <= e <= c+d1[c]-1 (just shrink the radius), of length 2*(e-c)+1 — so for fixed e we want the SMALLEST valid center c whose reach c+d1[c]-1 covers e, to maximize the length. Because 'reach covers e' can only become false as e grows (never true again once false), a single forward-moving pointer suffices: sweep e from 0 to n-1, and while the current candidate center's reach is less than e, advance the pointer. This is an O(n) amortized two-pointer sweep, done once for odd centers and once for even centers (which contribute even-length candidates of length 2*(e-c)+2 under the analogous condition), taking the max of both for each position.

subtopics.name: Trie for Strings (and Suffix Array/Automaton Basics)
subtopics.theory:
A trie (prefix tree) stores a set of strings by sharing common prefixes along root-to-node paths: each node has up to |alphabet| children, and a string is present in the set iff following its characters from the root lands on a node marked as an endpoint. Insertion and single-string lookup both cost O(length), and — crucially — a trie is the natural data structure the moment you have MANY patterns to search for simultaneously, since a single traversal of a text can match against every pattern sharing a prefix at once. Building a trie over all substrings (or all suffixes) of a string of length n also gives an easy, if O(n^2)-node in the worst case, way to count distinct substrings: it equals the number of nodes created (excluding the root).

The trie's real power for multi-pattern text search comes from turning it into the Aho-Corasick automaton: build the trie of all k patterns, then compute a 'failure link' for every node via BFS — analogous to the KMP failure function, but generalized to a tree of patterns instead of a single string — pointing to the longest proper suffix of the current node's path that is also a prefix of some pattern (i.e. also a node in the trie). Scanning the text once, moving along trie edges and falling back along failure links exactly like KMP, visits every position in O(1) amortized per character (with transitions precomputed, true O(1) per character), and a hit counter propagated along fail links after the scan yields, for every pattern, its total number of occurrences in the text — all in O(n + sum of pattern lengths) instead of running separate O(n) KMP passes per pattern.

When the patterns are the string's OWN suffixes rather than an external pattern set, the trie of suffixes becomes prohibitively large (O(n^2) nodes) but its compressed form is the suffix tree, and its array-based cousin is the suffix array: the starting indices of all suffixes, sorted lexicographically. A simple O(n log^2 n) construction sorts suffixes by successively doubling the compared prefix length, re-ranking pairs of previously-computed ranks each round. Once built, Kasai's algorithm computes the LCP array (longest common prefix between lexicographically adjacent suffixes) in O(n), which unlocks many classic queries: the number of distinct substrings is n(n+1)/2 minus the sum of the LCP array (every substring is a prefix of exactly one suffix, and the LCP array tells you exactly how much overlap/duplication exists between consecutive suffixes' prefixes). The suffix automaton is the further, more advanced step: a DAG with O(n) states representing every distinct substring implicitly, built online in O(n), and is generally the tool of choice once suffix-array-based solutions become too slow or intricate — well worth learning next, but its construction is sufficiently bug-prone that it deserves its own dedicated study session rather than a single worked example here.
subtopics.recognition: Use a plain trie whenever you're matching against a SET of patterns rather than one (prefix queries, autocomplete, or counting shared prefixes), and specifically reach for Aho-Corasick when you need to find occurrences of many patterns inside one text in a single pass. Reach for a suffix array/automaton once a problem needs global information about ALL substrings of a single string at once — counting distinct substrings, finding the k-th lexicographically smallest substring, or computing longest common substrings across strings — since those are awkward or too slow with hashing/tries alone at large n.
subtopics.complexity: Trie: O(total pattern length) to build, O(length) per query. Aho-Corasick: O(n + sum|pattern|) to build and scan. Suffix array (doubling): O(n log^2 n) to build, O(n) for the LCP array via Kasai's algorithm afterward.

examples.title: Counting Occurrences of Many Patterns (Aho-Corasick)
examples.problem: You are given a text string T (1 <= |T| <= 2*10^5) and k patterns (1 <= k <= 2*10^5, total pattern length up to 2*10^5), all lowercase Latin letters. For each pattern (in input order), output how many times it occurs in T (occurrences may overlap).
examples.approach: Insert all k patterns into a trie, recording the trie node reached at the end of each pattern. Build Aho-Corasick failure links with a BFS over the trie: for the root's children, missing transitions point back to the root; for deeper nodes, the failure link of a child reached via character c from node u is next[fail[u]][c] (computed level by level so fail[u] is already finalized), and non-existent transitions are patched to point directly at next[fail[u]][c] so the automaton has O(1) transitions everywhere (no need to walk fail chains during the scan). Scan T once, following automaton transitions and incrementing a hit counter at the current node for every character. Finally, propagate hit counts along failure links from deepest to shallowest node (any pattern ending at a fail-ancestor of a matched node also just matched, since that ancestor's string is a suffix of what was matched) so each pattern's end-node holds its true total occurrence count.

examples.title: Counting Distinct Substrings via Suffix Array + Kasai's LCP
examples.problem: Given a string s of length n (1 <= n <= 10^5), count the number of distinct substrings of s (substrings that are equal as sequences of characters are counted once, regardless of how many positions they occur at).
examples.approach: Every substring of s is a prefix of exactly one suffix. If we sort all n suffixes lexicographically (the suffix array) and look at consecutive suffixes in that sorted order, the number of NEW distinct prefixes contributed by the suffix at sorted position i is (length of that suffix) minus (its longest common prefix with the previous suffix in sorted order) — because any prefix shorter than or equal to that LCP was already counted as a prefix of the previous suffix. Build the suffix array with an O(n log^2 n) doubling algorithm (sort suffixes by (rank[i], rank[i+k]) pairs, doubling k each round), compute the LCP array between lexicographically adjacent suffixes with Kasai's O(n) algorithm, and the answer is n(n+1)/2 (total substrings, counted with multiplicity by (start,end) pairs) minus the sum of the LCP array (the total overcount from shared prefixes).
